To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
preterm, low-birthweight, and small-for-gestational-age deliveries are more common in women with a history of breast cancer than in the general population, especially in black women.
women with a previous breastcancer diagnosis were at higher risk for PTB, SGA, and LBW, and this risk was especially pronounced among black women.

women with a history of breast cancer are at higher risk of having preterm, low-birthweight, or small for gestational-age infants, especially if they receive chemotherapy or give birth within 2 years of their breast cancer diagnoses date.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the potential impact of breast cancer and its treatment on the reproductive health of young women.
the reproductive health outcomes of breast cancer survivors and the potential for disparities by race.
the health of women who have had a previous diagnosis of breast cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
women with a breast history are at higher risk for delivering a PTB/LBW/SGA infant compared to the general population and that the risk of a PTB is significantly modified by race.
women with breast cancer history have an increased risk of delivering preterm, low weight or small for gestational aged infants.
breast cancer history, particularly if it was diagnosed before the age of 35, was associated with increased risk for PTB and LBW.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the risk for adverse birth outcomes is higher in women with breast cancer history compared to those in general population and this risk may be even higher in women who have received chemotherapy and those who delivered their baby within 2 year of their breast cancer history.
breast cancer treatment may affect birth outcomes.
women with a breast history have higher rates of preterm birth and low birthweight infants.
The main takeaway from our work is that
women with a breast and reproductive age history of cancer may need additional counseling and care during pregnancy.
breast cancer survivors are at increased risk of delivering a preterm, low-birthweight, or small-for-gestational-age infant, and the effect is more pronounced for black mothers.
the risk of delivering an infant at less than 37 weeks gestation is significantly higher among black mothers with a breast cancer diagnosis history than among white mothers with a breast history.
